lesson.menu_desc: Beams, plaster and damp -- and the passive voice, which is how anybody actually talks about an old building
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 7 -- The House I Am Restoring
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Ana Claudia Veraldi | Lesson 7 -- The House I Am Restoring

listenings.text: The house was built in sixteen seventy-one and it has been repaired badly at least four times since then. When we bought it, the front wall was held up by two steel bars that were put there in the nineteen sixties, and nobody could tell us who had put them there. Everything downstairs was damp. The plaster was removed by hand, one square meter at a time, because a machine would have taken the brick with it. The beams turned out to be perfect. They were cut from one single tree, and they are sturdier than anything you can buy today. The electrics were done last winter and the whole house was rewired in eleven days, which is the only part of this project that went quickly. My advice, if anybody asks, is simple. Do not cut corners on the roof and do not believe anybody who tells you a number in the first week.

Ours is what we call a Queenslander, so the whole thing is built on posts, about two meters off the ground, and that is not decoration. It was designed that way so the air could move underneath. The place had been empty for twelve years when we got it. The verandah was rotten, the floor had been covered with three layers of vinyl, and somebody had painted every window shut. We stripped the floorboards ourselves and they were sanded down over about six weekends. That was the good part. The bad part was the roof, which had been done cheaply by the previous owner, and the whole thing had to be taken off and replaced. People call these houses a money pit and they are not wrong. But it was built to last, and once it is done properly, it is done for another hundred years.
